think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 40-year-old male with recurrent recent severe febrile illness presents with acute altered mental status, coma (GCS 12), and an emergent non-contrast CT head demonstrating an acute subdural hematoma with a 13-mm midline shift, in the complete absence of head trauma, seizures, anticoagulation, or baseline coagulopathy. Recognizing that cerebral microvascular sequestration, parasitized erythrocyte cytoadherence, and endothelial damage from Plasmodium falciparum can precipitate life-threatening spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage is critical.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The narrative concludes immediately following the initial emergency neurological evaluation, vital signs, baseline hematologic/metabolic/coagulation labs, and non-contrast head CT confirming the acute subdural hematoma with midline shift, prior to disclosing rapid malaria antigen testing, blood smear microscopy parasite counts, or emergency neurosurgical burr-hole evacuation.
3. Differential Distinctions: Traumatic subdural hematoma is the commonest etiology of subdural hemorrhage but is excluded by absence of trauma and sudden spontaneous onset. Spontaneous hematoma secondary to inherited/acquired coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia is ruled out by normal platelet count (349 x 10^9/L), normal PT/INR (1.16), and normal aPTT. Ruptured cerebral aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation can cause spontaneous intracranial bleeding, but typically produces subarachnoid hemorrhage and CT angiography demonstrated no vascular malformations. Severe falciparum infection causes microvascular sequestration, endothelial rupture, and spontaneous subdural bleeding.
case_prompt:
A 40-year-old male is admitted to the emergency department with a two-day history of progressively altered mental status culminating in loss of consciousness on the day of presentation. There is no history of preceding head trauma, falls, or seizures. Four days prior to this admission, the patient had been evaluated for an acute systemic febrile illness accompanied by severe headaches and generalized body malaise, for which he was receiving parenteral therapy. He has a history of two similar episodes of febrile illness in the past two months, making this his third acute episode. He has no chronic medical illnesses, no personal or family history of bleeding disorders or coagulopathies, and reports no history of tobacco or alcohol use.

On physical examination, the patient is obtunded with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 12 (Eye 3, Motor 6, Verbal 3). Vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 145/84 mmHg, pulse rate of 62 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute, body temperature of 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation of 98% while breathing ambient air. General examination reveals no external evidence of cranial injury, contusions, or cutaneous petechiae. Neurological examination reveals no signs of meningeal irritation or focal motor deficits.

Initial laboratory evaluations demonstrate a white blood cell count of 8.13 x 10^9/L (reference: 4–11 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin of 11.9 g/dL (reference: 11–16.5 g/dL), platelet count of 349 x 10^9/L (reference: 150–450 x 10^9/L), and C-reactive protein of 2.46 mg/dL (reference: <5 mg/dL). Renal and electrolyte values show a blood urea nitrogen of 4.6 mmol/L, serum creatinine of 51.36 umol/L, sodium of 133 mmol/L, potassium of 4.11 mmol/L, and chloride of 95.78 mmol/L. Liver function tests show a total bilirubin of 8.08 umol/L, direct bilirubin of 4.48 umol/L, AST of 14.2 IU/L, ALT of 33.58 IU/L, GGT of 91.73 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase of 50.98 IU/L. Coagulation profile shows a prothrombin time of 12.8 s, activated partial thromboplastin time of 30.7 s, and INR of 1.16. An emergent non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head reveals an acute left subdural hematoma with significant mass effect and a 13-mm midline shift.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Traumatic Subdural Hematoma or Occult Structural Vascular Malformation
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Subdural hematomas typically stem from blunt cranial trauma tearing bridging veins or from underlying vascular malformations; here, there was zero history or physical evidence of trauma, and CT angiography excluded underlying cerebral aneurysms or arteriovenous anomalies.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There was no trauma or seizures reported.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Spontaneous intracranial bleeding can arise from severe thrombocytopenia, hemophilia, or liver-related coagulopathy; however, the patient's platelet count and complete coagulation panel were entirely within normal limits, and he had no family or personal history of coagulopathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There is no history of chronic illnesses, and there is no personal or family history of coagulopathies.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Rapid antigen testing and peripheral blood examination demonstrated high-burden Plasmodium falciparum infection, establishing parasitic microvascular sequestration, localized capillary obstruction, and endothelial breakdown as the causative mechanism of the acute subdural hemorrhage.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The rapid test for malaria antigen was positive for plasmodium falciparum with a parasite count of 50 trophozoites per 200 white blood cells.

editor_comments: Case prompt strictly stops at the admission head CT. Zero mention of malaria, plasmodium, artesunate, or rapid antigen testing in the clinical presentation. Exact verbatim quotes validated.
